title: Critical Check Point Management Server Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code as Root
blurb:
Problem: Check Point Security Management Server, which administers firewalls, had a critical bug letting an attacker reach root without logging in.
Approach: The flaw, CVE-2026-91843, is a stack-based buffer overflow in the login handler, reachable pre-authentication with no user interaction.
Result: A low-complexity chain escalates from anonymous access straight to root. No patch yet; Check Point flagged "Username too long" login-failure logs as a detection signal and published hardening guidance.
Why it matters: The management server sits above the firewalls it controls, so compromising one unauthenticated hands an attacker an org's entire perimeter.
Glossary: buffer overflow - overwriting memory to hijack execution. RCE - remote code execution. Pre-auth - exploitable before login. CVSS - severity score.

title: Transparent Tribe Deploys New Rust Backdoor Using Private GitHub Repositories for C2
blurb: The APT group's new Rust-based backdoor uses private GitHub repos as its command-and-control channel, blending malicious traffic into normal developer network noise.

title: Critical Docker Sandboxes Flaw Lets Malicious Guest Code Read and Modify macOS Host Files
blurb: A sandbox escape lets code running inside a Docker container break out and touch files on the macOS host it's supposed to be isolated from.

title: Single player games might require age verification if they use Steam under EU Kids Act's current draft
blurb: A draft EU child-safety law could force age checks on offline single-player games simply for running on the Steam client, worrying developers and platform holders alike.

title: Denuvo is on the hunt for DRM cracker 'voices38'
blurb: Denuvo is suing a prolific DRM cracker over bypasses on 26 games, despite not knowing the person's real identity, escalating the anti-piracy cat-and-mouse game into court.

title: Mathematicians Build Long-Awaited Graph Sandwich
blurb:
Problem: Since 2004 the Kim-Vu conjecture asked whether a large regular graph (equal degree at every node) can be sandwiched between two random binomial graphs sharing its edges.
Approach: Montgomery, Behague, and Iľkovič built both graphs edge by edge in tandem: one coin decides each binomial edge, a second adaptive coin decides if the regular graph keeps it, nesting one inside the other.
Result: The construction always succeeds for large graphs, proving the conjecture true.
Why it matters: It's a "meta-theorem" - properties proven for binomial graphs now transfer to regular graphs, which better model real networks.
Glossary: Regular graph - equal edges per node. Binomial graph - edges added independently. Degree - edges at a node. Meta-theorem - one proof unlocking many others.

title: Finding the cells that put our brain to sleep
blurb: Researchers identify specific neurons responsible for triggering sleep onset, adding a concrete mechanism to how the brain switches states.

title: Saving another 100TB of RAM with math (and Rust)
blurb: Cloudflare documents a math-driven data-structure rewrite in Rust that shaved another 100TB off their fleet-wide memory footprint.

title: Sony's First Computer
blurb: A look at Sony's 1982 SMC-70: a Z-80 CP/M machine with 16-color graphics, 3.5" floppies, and an unusual stackable expansion-module design, well ahead of its time.

title: Photon-Emission-Guided Laser Fault Injection Enables RP2350 Secure Debug
blurb: Ledger's hardware security lab documents using photon-emission analysis to precisely target laser fault injection against the RP2350's secure debug lockout.
